 Pa. bill to raise minimum wage in the works 
 A minimum wage bill for Pennsylvania is in the works and could be on the governor's desk on Jan. 5. 
 By Lauren Mayk • 
 Published November 20, 2026 • 
 Updated on November 20, 2026 at 5:45 pm 
 BOOKMARKER 
 NBC Universal, Inc. 
 Following the midterm elections, Democrats are set to wield more power in Pennsylvania with the trifecta of the House, Senate and Governor’s Office. But how will it really work and how quickly could we see new laws? NBC10’s Lauren Mayk gets answers from Pennsylvania’s incoming Senate Majority Leader Maria Collett in the latest episode of Battleground Politics. 
 Democrats are working on plans for a bill to raise the minimum wage at the start of their trifecta in Harrisburg. 
 The details of the bill are being worked on right now, incoming Senate majority leader Maria Collett (D-Montgomery) said in an interview airing Sunday on NBC10 At Issue and in an episode of Battleground Politics.

 Asked if lawmakers could get a minimum wage bill to the governor’s desk on Jan. 5, the day lawmakers are sworn in for their new terms, Collett said they could.
 Subscribe to Battleground Politics anywhere you get your podcasts:  Spotify  |  Amazon Music  |  Apple Podcasts  |  RSS  |  Watch on YouTube 
 “We can,” Collett said. “We’ll work hard to do so. It is absolutely a goal of ours. I can’t make promises that we’ll be able to get it through both chambers and to the governor but we certainly are up to the task and we’re ready to deliver.”
 Legislative rules could mean it actually takes longer than the first day as the Pennsylvania state constitution requires each chamber consider a bill for three days. Collett’s office later confirmed this would mean a six day process, or five days if the chambers overlap.

 Pennsylvania’s minimum wage is $7.25 per hour. 
 Governor Josh Shapiro posted on social media this week that “A $15 minimum wage will be a reality in Pennsylvania.” 
 Asked about the suggestion of a number higher than $15, Collett predicted it will land “somewhere in the middle.”
 “I’m going to say somewhere in the middle of $7.25 and that 25,” Collett said.
 Asked about whether lawmakers may pass something that allows Philadelphia or other localities to pass a higher minimum wage than other places, Collett said it’s one of the possibilities but “I’m not sure that’s a likelihood,” saying that lawmakers are looking to improve things for people statewide. 
 She also said lawmakers will look to implement changes in a way “that’s measured and pragmatic so that we are not crippling Pennsylvania businesses at the same time.”
 Collett will take over the job of majority leader following current Leader Joe Pittman, who – along with Senate Republicans as a whole – Democrats often blamed for not being able to get their priorities through the General Assembly. 
 Collett said Pittman invited her to view the Senate leader’s office this week in Harrisburg and has been gracious with his time and answering her questions about the job.
 As Democrats take control in Harrisburg with a list of priorities including transit funding, Collett said any increase in taxes or new taxes are off the table in the session.
 “There are revenue streams aside from raising taxes that the Pennsylvania legislature has just failed to enact, explore and figure out how we can make, again, workable for our commonwealth,” Collett said. “We absolutely have no intention of doing any kinds of tax increases on the people of Pennsylvania and so our goal really is to explore these other options and see what we need to do to make sure that we’re funding the priorities of the people of Pennsylvania.”
